issues.legal_issue: A limited-tenancy permission is not invalidated as fraudulent merely because the landlord has previously obtained permissions for other limited lettings, where the alleged abuse is unsupported by adequate factual evidence.
material_facts: The landlord sought permission to let part of a house for a limited residential period and explained that he was living in government accommodation and needed to allow for the possibility that it might be cancelled.
The tenant accepted the landlord’s statement and undertook to vacate when the agreed period ended.

Although the tenant alleged that the landlord had obtained similar permissions for other lettings, the tenant did not cross-examine the landlord about those lettings or provide independent evidence that they involved abuse of the law.

There was no material before the Rent Controller establishing or arousing suspicion of fraud, and repeated limited lettings did not necessarily show that the premises had been available for indefinite letting.
issues.conclusion: The allegation of fraud was not established, and the permission was not vitiated on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: A fraud allegation is a mixed question of fact and law and requires a factual foundation showing wilful contravention or abuse. Under Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, the limited tenancy must be bona fide, for residential purposes, and supported by the Controller’s permission; the landlord’s statement must be bona fide and there must be no fraud or collusion, though the permission is presumed regular. S.B. Noronah v. Prem Kumari Khanna was applied; V.S. Rahi v. Ram Chambeli was distinguished because it involved false declarations; and Dhanwanti v. D.D. Gupta was relied on for the principle that repeated limited lettings do not by themselves establish that the premises were available indefinitely.

rule.if: limited_tenancy_possession_execution and fraud_alleged and (fraud_evidence_absent or repeated_limited_lettings_only)

predicates.limited_tenancy_possession_execution: The proceeding seeks possession after a tenancy granted for a limited period has ended.
predicates.fraud_alleged: The tenant alleged that the landlord obtained the limited-tenancy permission by abusing the law.
predicates.fraud_evidence_absent: The tenant did not provide adequate evidence establishing that the landlord’s conduct involved fraud or abuse.
predicates.repeated_limited_lettings_only: The allegation of abuse rested on the landlord having made other limited lettings, without proof that those lettings were fraudulent.

issues.definition: When possession is sought after a limited tenancy and the fraud allegation lacks supporting evidence or rests only on repeated limited lettings, the permission is not invalidated for fraud.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s failure to challenge alleged fraud during the limited tenancy weakens a later challenge raised after the tenancy has ended.
material_facts: The tenant waited until the full agreed tenancy period had expired before raising the allegation that the permission had been obtained by fraud.
The tenant did not seek a determination from the Rent Controller during the tenancy after the alleged circumstances became known.
issues.conclusion: The delay weakened the tenant’s objection and deprived it of force and content; the tenant should have approached the Rent Controller during the limited tenancy after discovering circumstances said to vitiate the permission.
issues.legal_principle: J.R. Vohra v. India Export House states that a tenant alleging ritualistic compliance, fraud, or collusion in obtaining permission for a limited tenancy should approach the Rent Controller during that tenancy, as soon as the relevant circumstances are discovered, rather than wait until the landlord seeks possession after expiry.

predicates.limited_tenancy_possession_execution: The proceeding seeks possession after a tenancy granted for a limited period has ended.
predicates.fraud_objection_raised_after_expiry: The tenant first raised the allegation of fraud after the agreed limited tenancy had expired.

issues.definition: When a tenant raises an alleged-fraud objection only after the limited tenancy has ended in a possession proceeding, the late objection is weakened.

issues.legal_issue: Permission for a limited tenancy is not invalid merely because the parties did not execute a separate written lease after the permission was granted.
material_facts: The parties made and signed statements before the Rent Controller setting out the proposed limited residential tenancy and its terms, and a draft lease was submitted.
The Rent Controller granted permission on the basis of the application and the parties’ statements.
The tenant argued that no separate written lease had been executed after permission was granted.
The Delhi High Court had consistently treated the statutory procedure as a complete code and had held that no separate post-permission agreement was required.
issues.conclusion: The signed statements and the material before the Rent Controller sufficiently complied with the requirement; the absence of a separate written lease did not invalidate the permission or defeat the possession proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, was treated as a complete code by the established interpretation of the Delhi High Court. The Court adhered to that settled interpretation of a local statute to avoid uncertainty and disruption of transactions made in reliance on it. It relied on Kasturi Lal v. Shiv Charan Das Mathur, Raj Narain Pandey v. Sant Prasad Tewari, and its decision in Inder Mohan Lal v. Ramesh Khanna.

predicates.limited_tenancy_possession_execution: The proceeding seeks possession under a tenancy granted for a limited period with the Rent Controller’s permission.
predicates.signed_controller_statements_set_out_ter: The parties signed statements before the Controller that set out the terms of the proposed tenancy.
predicates.local_high_court_interpretation_long_set: The local High Court had consistently applied an interpretation under which the permission procedure did not require a separate written lease after permission was granted.

issues.definition: When signed statements set out the tenancy terms in a possession proceeding and the local interpretation has long been settled, the permission remains valid without a separate written lease.
